Overcoming Frequency Resolution Limits Using a Solid-State Spin Quantum Sensor

Demonstrates superresolution quantum sensing that resolves two nearly identical incoherent signals with a solid-state spin quantum sensor by choosing interrogation times satisfying a superresolution condition, improving scaling from t^-1 to t^-2.
Very relevant to the “break the apparent resolution limit” theme; not superconducting-specific, but conceptually close to spectroscopy beyond naive linewidth/coherence constraints.
Enhanced coherence of all-nitride superconducting qubits epitaxially grown on silicon substrate

Improving the coherence of superconducting qubits is a fundamental step towards the realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, coherence times of quantum circuits made from conventional aluminum-based Josephson junctions are limited by the presence of microscopic two-level systems in the amorphous aluminum oxide tunnel barriers. Here, we have developed superconducting qubits based on NbN/AlN/NbN epitaxial Josephson junctions on silicon substrates which promise to overcome the drawbacks of qubits based on Al/AlOx/Al junctions. The all-nitride qubits have great advantages such as chemical stability against oxidation, resulting in fewer two-level fluctuators, feasibility for epitaxial tunnel barriers that reduce energy relaxation and dephasing, and a larger superconducting gap of \~5.2 meV for NbN, compared to \~0.3 meV for aluminum, which suppresses the excitation of quasiparticles. By replacing conventional MgO by a silicon substrate with a TiN buffer layer for epitaxial growth of nitride junctions, we demonstrate a qubit energy relaxation time \$\$\T\_\1\=16.3$ackslash$;\\$ackslash$upmu \\\\\\\$ackslash$rm\s\\\\\\\$\$and a spin-echo dephasing time \$\$\T\_\2\=21.5$ackslash$;\\$ackslash$upmu \\\\\\\$ackslash$rm\s\\\\\\\$\$. These significant improvements in quantum coherence are explained by the reduced dielectric loss compared to the previously reported \$\$\T\_\1\$ackslash$approx \T\_\2\$ackslash$approx 0.5$ackslash$;\\$ackslash$upmu \\\\\\\$ackslash$rm\s\\\\\\\$\$of NbN-based qubits on MgO substrates. These results are an important step towards constructing a new platform for superconducting quantum hardware.
Coherent control of a hybrid superconducting circuit made with graphene-based van der Waals heterostructures

Quantum coherence and control is foundational to the science and engineering of quantum systems1,2. In van der Waals materials, the collective coherent behaviour of carriers has been probed successfully by transport measurements3–6. However, temporal coherence and control, as exemplified by manipulating a single quantum degree of freedom, remains to be verified. Here we demonstrate such coherence and control of a superconducting circuit incorporating graphene-based Josephson junctions. Furthermore, we show that this device can be operated as a voltage-tunable transmon qubit7–9, whose spectrum reflects the electronic properties of massless Dirac fermions travelling ballistically4,5. In addition to the potential for advancing extensible quantum computing technology, our results represent a new approach to studying van der Waals materials using microwave photons in coherent quantum circuits.
Limits on Spectral Resolution Measurements by Quantum Probes

Analyzes frequency-resolution limits in nano-NMR and shows theoretically and experimentally that resolving nearby frequencies and estimating a single frequency are both governed by the Cramer-Rao bound, refining the usual intuition about fixed signal-timescale limits.
Important for literature review framing: challenges simple claims that two-frequency resolution is absolutely fixed by a single decay/coherence timescale.
Overcoming resolution limits with quantum sensing

The field of quantum sensing explores the use of quantum phenomena to measure a broad range of physical quantities, of both static and time-dependent types. While for static signals the main figure of merit is sensitivity, for time dependent signals it is spectral resolution, i.e. the ability to resolve two different frequencies. Here we study this problem, and develop new superresolution methods that rely on quantum features. We first formulate a general criterion for superresolution in quantum problems. Inspired by this, we show that quantum detectors can resolve two frequencies from incoherent segments of the signal, irrespective of their separation, in contrast to what is known about classical detection schemes. The main idea behind these methods is to overcome the vanishing distinguishability in resolution problems by nullifying the projection noise.
Power narrowing: counteracting Doppler broadening in two-color transitions

Doppler broadening in thermal ensembles degrades the absorption cross-section and the coherence time of collective excitations. In two photon transitions, it is common to assume that this problem becomes worse with larger wavelength mismatch. Here we identify an opposite mechanism, where such wavelength mismatch leads to cancellation of Doppler broadening via the counteracting effects of velocity-dependent light-shifts and Doppler shifts. We show that this effect is general, common to both absorption and transparency resonances, and favorably scales with wavelength mismatch. We experimentally confirm the enhancement of transitions for different low-lying orbitals in rubidium atoms and use calculations to extrapolate to high-lying Rydberg orbitals. These calculations predict a dramatic enhancement of up to 20-fold increase in absorption, even in the presence of large homogeneous broadening. More general configurations, where an auxiliary dressing field is used to counteract Doppler broadening, are also discussed and experimentally demonstrated. The mechanism we study can be applied as well for rephasing of spin waves and increasing the coherence time of quantum memories.
Important for literature review terminology: same phrase, different mechanism from Lorentzian-pulse power narrowing. Useful to avoid conflating meanings.

Demonstration of qubit operations below a rigorous fault tolerance threshold with gate set tomography

Quantum information processors promise fast algorithms for problems inaccessible to classical computers. But since qubits are noisy and error-prone, they will depend on fault-tolerant quantum error correction (FTQEC) to compute reliably. Quantum error correction can protect against general noise if—and only if—the error in each physical qubit operation is smaller than a certain threshold. The threshold for general errors is quantified by their diamond norm. Until now, qubits have been assessed primarily by randomized benchmarking, which reports a different error rate that is not sensitive to all errors, and cannot be compared directly to diamond norm thresholds. Here we use gate set tomography to completely characterize operations on a trapped-Yb+-ion qubit and demonstrate with greater than 95\% confidence that they satisfy a rigorous threshold for FTQEC (diamond norm ≤6.7 ×10−4).
Power narrowing in coherent atomic excitation by smoothly shaped pulsed fields

When atoms are excited by laser radiation the conventional wisdom dictates that the spectral excitation profile – the excited-state population vs the detuning – broadens as the radiation intensity increases. This common expectation has been shown to be incorrect in the fluorescence signal following two-photon excitation of xenon atoms by a Gaussian laser pulse, which showed almost no power broadening [T. Halfmann, T. Rickes, N.V. Vitanov, K. Bergmann, Optics Communications, 220 (2003) 353] Here we go a step further and show that for a class of pulse shapes, the falling edges of which vanish as inverse powers of time, ∝t−n (with n>1), the spectral excitation profile must exhibit power narrowing, i.e. the spectral linewidth scales as Ω0−1/(n−1), where Ω0 is the Rabi frequency of the transition. We provide a simple physical explanation based upon the notions of adiabatic evolution and coherent population return and discuss important experimental applications.
Important cited reference: likely the key theoretical ancestor of the PRL power-narrowing result. Read before/with paper 25.

We compare lineshapes obtained in laser-induced fluorescence and resonantly enhanced multi-photon ionisation, resulting from coherent pulsed excitation of a two-photon transition in xenon atoms. We find that excitation profiles probed by ionisation show power broadening as expected. Here ionisation occurs simultaneously with the coherent excitation. The profiles observed by fluorescence show almost no broadening, because of coherent population return, since the fluorescence occurs predominantly after the excitation pulse is over. Thus the observed lineshape depends characteristically upon the nature of the probing process.
Power broadening revisited: theory and experiment

The spectral width of an atomic absorption line, observed with a steady light source, typically increases as the light intensity increases, an effect known as power broadening. In this paper, we point out classes of pulsed-light observations where power broadening does not always occur. We present analytical and numerical results, supported by experimental data of coherent pulsed excitation probed by photoionization, which show that the extent of power broadening depends crucially upon the nature of excitation and the type of measurement. In particular, we show that a spectral line obtained from measurement performed after pulsed excitation exhibits no power broadening. For pulsed excitation and continuous measurement, the spectral line contains two components: a power-broadened signal collected during the excitation and an unbroadened signal collected after the excitation.

Breaking the diffraction resolution limit by stimulated emission: stimulated-emission-depletion fluorescence microscopy

We propose a new type of scanning fluorescence microscope capable of resolving 35 nm in the far field. We overcome the diffraction resolution limit by employing stimulated emission to inhibit the fluorescence process in the outer regions of the excitation point-spread function. In contrast to near-field scanning optical microscopy, this method can produce three-dimensional images of translucent specimens.

L Allen and J H Eberly Chichester: J Wiley 1975 pp xiii + 233 price £10.80 (cased) Allen and Eberly, who have been most actively engaged in the expanding field of laser physics have written this introduction to optical resonance, pulse propagation and superradiance and allied phenomena relying mainly on quasiclassical methods. The mathematical apparatus and the actual, minimal, amount of quantum electrodynamics put to use, should make this text accessible to every graduate physicist.

The extension of maser techniques to the infrared and optical region is considered. It is shown that by using a resonant cavity of centimeter dimensions, having many resonant modes, maser oscillation at these wavelengths can be achieved by pumping with reasonable amounts of incoherent light. For wavelengths much shorter than those of the ultraviolet region, maser-type amplification appears to be quite impractical. Although use of a multimode cavity is suggested, a single mode may be selected by making only the end walls highly reflecting, and defining a suitably small angular aperture. Then extremely monochromatic and coherent light is produced. The design principles are illustrated by reference to a system using potassium vapor.

A nanoscale magnetic spectrum analyzer based on qubit dressed states
Develops a nanoscale magnetic spectrum analyzer based on qubit dressed states, targeting broad spectral bandwidth, high sensitivity, and nanoscale spatial resolution with NV centers.
Adjacent but relevant to your dressed/adiabatic-basis and spectroscopy interests: spectroscopy through engineered qubit dressed states.
Assessing Spatiotemporally Correlated Noise in Superconducting Qubits via Pulse-Based Quantum Noise Spectroscopy

Proposes and validates a nonparametric quantum noise spectroscopy protocol for estimating spectra and static errors associated with spatiotemporally correlated dephasing noise and fluctuating quantum crosstalk on two superconducting qubits.
Strong 2026 hardware-context paper: pulse-based spectroscopy on superconducting qubits, relevant to echo/filter-function thinking and multi-qubit calibration.

Pedagogical introduction to pulse-shaping techniques for transmon qubits, covering pulse envelopes, spectral properties, finite bandwidth, leakage, DRAG, Magnus-expansion intuition, hardware realities of AWGs/LOs/IQ mixing, and extensions to two-qubit operations.
Strong 2026 fit for your project: tutorial-level map of pulse shaping in exactly your hardware platform. Useful for literature-review framing and terminology.
Superresolution in Quantum Noise Spectroscopy via Filter Design

Uses filter-function quantum control theory to derive analytic conditions for quantum sensing protocols that achieve superresolution: discriminating spectral lines with arbitrarily small frequency separation.
Very relevant to the T2/resolution-limit thread. It connects superresolution directly to filter design/control protocols rather than just post-processing.
Time-Reversal and Reversible Dynamics in Cavity QED for Quantum Metrology

Reviews and develops time-reversal/reversible dynamics in cavity QED for quantum-enhanced metrology, emphasizing that many-body interactions can generate entangled states and can also be reversed to extract metrological advantage with realistic measurements.
Fresh July 2026 paper. Adjacent rather than superconducting-specific, but useful for the Loschmidt/time-reversal measurement layer of the project.
Observation of Power Superbroadening of Spectral Line Profiles on IBM Quantum

Follow-up IBM Quantum study of shaped pulses that intentionally produce spectral line profiles with power broadening greater than rectangular pulses, contrasting with Lorentzian-pulse power narrowing and surveying pulse-shape dependence of spectral response.
Useful comparison paper: not power narrowing itself, but highly relevant for distinguishing pulse families that narrow versus broaden spectral profiles under stronger driving.
Defying Conventional Wisdom in Spectroscopy: Power Narrowing on IBM Quantum

Power narrowing is demonstrated experimentally for powers-of-Lorentzian pulse shapes on the IBM Quantum processor ibmq_manila. The line width is reduced by over a factor of 10 when increasing pulse area from pi to 7 pi, and the work analyzes truncation of pulse wings and cut-off broadening.
Strong direct fit: Lorentzian shaped pulses, IBM superconducting-qubit hardware, amplitude-dependent linewidth narrowing, and truncation effects relevant to root-Lorentzian/echo spectroscopy.
Qubit dynamics driven by smooth pulses of finite duration

Study of qubit dynamics under smooth finite-duration pulses whose shapes start and end linearly in time. The work reports much weaker power broadening, faster vanishing wings in excitation line profiles, reduced sidebands, analytic approximations, and agreement with IBM Quantum processor data.
Very relevant adjacent paper: not Lorentzian power narrowing, but directly about shaped qubit pulses, reduced power broadening, line-profile wings, and IBM Quantum experiments.
Controlling the uncontrollable: Quantum control of open system dynamics
Develops control of open quantum systems using a thermodynamically consistent framework where the drive modifies the system-environment interaction and dissipation depends on the control protocol.
Broader background, not spectroscopy-specific. Relevant for thinking about shaped pulses in a drive-dressed basis where dissipation and control are not separable.
Experimental demonstration of composite pulses on IBM's quantum computer

Experimental tests of broadband, narrowband, passband, and universal composite pulse sequences on an IBM superconducting transmon processor using low-level pulse control. The paper reports excitation profiles for many target probabilities and observes pronounced narrowband profiles.
Strong fit for your robust spectroscopy/control angle: experimental IBM transmon pulse-control data with narrowband and passband excitation profiles.
Variational Quantum Metrology with Loschmidt Echo

Uses a symmetric variational quantum circuit, analogous to a Loschmidt echo with forward and backward evolution, to estimate quantum Fisher information and demonstrate quantum metrology advantages on a 10-spin processor.
Modern implementation-oriented Loschmidt echo/metrology paper; useful for discussing echo signals as sensitivity-enhancing measurement protocols.
Correlated noise in Brownian motion allows for super resolution
Studies nano-NMR frequency resolution when diffusion broadening would normally limit spectral lines, showing that correlated diffusion noise can produce high spectral resolution in NV-based nano-NMR.
Related background, lower priority: useful for the broader idea that correlated measurements/noise models can beat simple linewidth-resolution expectations.
Precise Spectroscopy of High-Frequency Oscillating Fields with a Single-Qubit Sensor

Proposes measuring fast-oscillating-field frequency with a single-qubit sensor by using a stable classical clock and phase correlations between successive measurements, while integrating dynamical decoupling to suppress slow environmental noise.
Good bridge to superconducting qubit ideas: repeated qubit-sensor interrogations plus clocked phase correlations rather than relying on one long coherent probe evolution.
Achieving the ultimate precision limit in quantum NMR spectroscopy

Shows that the ultimate precision limit for estimating the Larmor frequency of unentangled spins can still be reached in quantum nano-NMR spectroscopy despite practical limitations of weak external probes, using appropriate control and measurement.
Useful limit paper for discussing what spectroscopy can recover with optimized control/measurement even when direct addressing/readout assumptions fail.
Experimental verification of the inertial theorem control protocols

Experimental validation of inertial-theorem control protocols in a trapped Ytterbium ion SU(2) system. The work demonstrates non-adiabatic driven solutions that bridge sudden and adiabatic limits and are stable to small deviations.
Useful because it translates the inertial/adiabatic-basis idea into a controlled two-level experimental system, closer to qubit spectroscopy than purely formal theory.
Inertial Theorem: Overcoming the Quantum Adiabatic Limit

Introduces the inertial theorem for driven quantum systems: stable solutions can remain valid for fast driving when acceleration is slow, extending adiabatic-style reasoning beyond the strict slow-driving limit using Liouville-space eigenoperators and geometric phases.
Most relevant Kosloff paper for your “adiabatic basis but not necessarily slow” question. Useful conceptual background for describing shaped pulses in a moving/effective basis.
Robust high-fidelity coherent control of two-state systems by detuning pulses

Develops high-fidelity coherent control using sequences of detuning pulses. The detuning pulse areas are used as control parameters, yielding broadband and narrowband transition probability profiles by analogy with composite pulses.
Useful theory bridge for shaped spectroscopy: narrowband transition profiles controlled through detuning pulses rather than only amplitude envelopes.
Time Dependent Markovian Quantum Master Equation

Constructs a Markovian master equation for externally driven open quantum systems using an explicit propagator solution. The resulting non-adiabatic master equation extends validity beyond the adiabatic limit and couples populations and coherences.
Relevant if your shaped spectroscopy pulses need an open-system description where the drive modifies the effective basis and population/coherence dynamics.
Proposes a Loschmidt echo protocol for quantum metrology, using forward and reversed dynamics to extract quantum Fisher information and quantify multiparticle entanglement.
Useful conceptual parallel: time reversal/echo signal as a metrological observable. Not superconducting-specific, but relevant for echo-as-spectroscopy framing.
Quantum spectroscopy of single spins assisted by a classical clock

Develops a correlation spectroscopy technique for quantum signals where performance is limited by target-spin coherence and clock stability rather than by the shorter coherence time of the quantum probe.
Central fit for T2-limit breaking: explicitly argues that probe coherence need not be the main resolution limit when phase correlations are tracked with a stable clock.
Rotating-frame relaxation as a noise spectrum analyzer of a superconducting qubit undergoing driven evolution

Demonstrates noise spectroscopy of a superconducting flux qubit during driven evolution using rotating-frame relaxation and spin-locking. Complements free-evolution methods and identifies a defect signature in time-domain spin-echo experiments.
Good fit for your shaped-drive spectroscopy context: spectroscopy during driven evolution, not just free Ramsey/Hahn evolution.
Arbitrarily accurate passband composite pulses for dynamical suppression of amplitude noise

Introduces passband composite pulse sequences built from broadband and narrowband composite sequences. The pulse profiles can be tuned in width and rectangularity, suppress excitation near pulse areas 0 and 2 pi, and suppress deviations from inversion near pi to high order for amplitude-noise robustness.
Relevant to amplitude robustness and controllable profile width; useful background for framing root-Lorentzian/echo pulse robustness against amplitude variation.
Control of qubits by shaped pulses of finite duration

Analyzes qubit control by shaped pulses of finite duration, providing pulse-shape and two-state-system background relevant to excitation profiles, linewidth control, and practical finite-pulse implementations.
Important cited background for translating power-narrowing pulse-shape ideas into qubit-control language.
Avoiding power broadening in optically detected magnetic resonance of single NV defects for enhanced dc magnetic field sensitivity

Shows how avoiding power broadening in optically detected magnetic resonance of single NV centers improves dc magnetic-field sensitivity. Useful as a high-impact example of power broadening as a practical spectroscopy limitation.
High-citation cited reference. Different platform, but useful for motivation: narrower driven resonance improves metrological/spectroscopic sensitivity.
Dynamical decoupling and noise spectroscopy with a superconducting flux qubit

Demonstrates dynamical decoupling and noise spectroscopy with a superconducting flux qubit. CPMG sequences improve coherence and act as filters for reconstructing the environmental noise power spectral density.
Very relevant hardware-context paper: echo/CPMG as spectroscopy/filtering in superconducting qubits.
Effects of pulse shape on strongly driven two-level systems
Studies how pulse shape affects strongly driven two-level systems, giving relevant background for excitation line profiles, sidebands, and deviations from simple rectangular-pulse intuition.
Important cited background for comparing rectangular, Gaussian, Lorentzian, and other shaped pulses under strong drive.
Trace Isotope Detection Enhanced by Coherent Elimination of Power Broadening

Demonstrates a spectroscopy approach where coherent effects eliminate power broadening, improving trace isotope detection. Relevant as a prior strategy for high-resolution spectroscopy under stronger driving.
Important cited comparison point: power broadening can be eliminated by coherent spectroscopy mechanisms, separate from Lorentzian-pulse power narrowing.
Fluorescence microscopy with diffraction resolution barrier broken by stimulated emission
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
Experimental demonstration of STED fluorescence microscopy breaking the diffraction resolution barrier by stimulated emission depletion.
Canonical STED demonstration. Useful as an analogy for engineered depletion/suppression around a narrow surviving response.
First observation of a photon echo, demonstrating optical-frequency rephasing analogous to spin echo in an inhomogeneously broadened transition.
Good historical bridge from spin echo to spectroscopy: echo refocusing as a way to recover narrow coherent response from inhomogeneous broadening.
Effects of Diffusion on Free Precession in Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Experiments
Classic Carr-Purcell echo paper extending spin-echo refocusing with repeated pulses, forming the basis for CPMG-style sequences and many later dynamical-decoupling spectroscopy methods.
Background for echo trains and filter-function/noise-spectroscopy thinking; useful if your method is framed against echo or CPMG style refocusing.

Foundational paper introducing spin echoes: refocusing dephased spin magnetization through pulse sequences, establishing the basic echo idea used throughout magnetic resonance and coherent spectroscopy.
Foundational echo paper. Useful for explaining the phase-refocusing intuition behind echo-style spectroscopy pulses.
